hero.name: Sunil
hero.who: a 29-year-old cab driver in Bengaluru whose earnings vanish every month

story.b: Sunil drives a cab in Bengaluru, mostly airport runs and late office drops along Outer Ring Road. Some months he earns well, some months less. Either way, by the twentieth, his wallet and his bank account are nearly empty. He sends money home to his parents in Mandya, pays the car loan and the room rent in Marathahalli, and the rest simply disappears. Tea, snacks at dhabas, biryani at midnight, a phone recharge, a loan to a friend. His wife Kavya asks how much they have saved for their daughter's school fees. Sunil opens his banking app at a signal near Silk Board and stares at the balance. It is four hundred and twelve rupees.

ask.q: Sunil has four hundred rupees left before the month ends. What is the most helpful way to see his problem?
o: He simply needs a higher-paying job before anything can change
His money habits matter more than his income, and habits can change
It was an unlucky month and the next one will be better
ask.why: Many people with bigger incomes are just as broke by the twentieth, because spending grows to match earnings. Hoping for luck or a better job leaves the leak open. Seeing that his habits decide where the money goes gives him something he can change right now.

chapters.take: Money problems are often habit problems, and habits can be changed.

story.b: Every Monday, the cab app sends Sunil his weekly payout. This time, before he buys even a cup of tea, he moves one tenth of it into a separate savings account that Kavya helped him open, with no card attached. The first week it is only eight hundred rupees. It feels like money taken from his own pocket. By Thursday he notices he has spent less on small things, simply because the main account looks smaller. He does not feel poorer. By the end of the month, the separate account holds over three thousand rupees, more than he has kept aside in a long time. He keeps the passbook in the glovebox and looks at it at red lights.

ask.q: Sunil's weekly payout has just arrived. What should he do first?
o: Move a fixed tenth into his separate savings account before spending
Pay all his bills, then save whatever remains on Sunday
Spend freely this week and save double next week
ask.why: Taking a fixed part out first makes saving automatic and keeps it safe from small daily spending. Saving after the bills usually leaves very little, and promising to save double later is easy to break when next week comes.

chapters.take: Pay yourself first. A fixed slice of every payout belongs to your future.

story.b: During the festival rush, Sunil earns more than ever. The extra money brings ideas with it. His friend Ganesh shows off a new phone bought on easy EMI and says Sunil deserves one too. Sunil's old phone works fine, though the screen has a crack in one corner. That night, waiting in the airport queue, he writes his last ten expenses in a notebook and marks each one need or want. Fuel, need. Rent, need. Midnight biryani three times, want. A second phone cover, want. The list surprises him. Many wants had quietly dressed up as needs. He decides the new phone can wait, and gets the cracked screen repaired for six hundred rupees instead.

ask.q: Sunil earned extra this month and a friend says he deserves an expensive new phone. What should he do?
o: Buy it on EMI, since the monthly amount is small
Upgrade, since a bigger income should mean a better lifestyle
Ask whether it is a true need, and repair his working phone instead
ask.why: Expenses quietly grow to match income, and an EMI makes a want feel cheap. Separating real needs from wants lets him choose on purpose. Repairing the working phone meets the need, while the upgrade would turn one good month into a new monthly cost.

chapters.take: Spending grows with income unless you choose what truly counts as a need.

story.b: After four months, Sunil's savings account holds a decent amount, but it just sits there. His cousin Divya, who works at a bank in Mysuru, explains a simple idea over a phone call on a slow Sunday. Each rupee he saves can be put to work, and what it earns can be put to work too. She tells him about recurring deposits, fixed deposits and SIPs in low-cost index funds, and warns that none of them is a get-rich plan. Sunil spends the next week reading about them in Kannada during his breaks. He keeps an emergency amount in his savings account and starts a small monthly SIP for his daughter's future, planning to leave it for many years.

ask.q: Sunil has steady savings sitting idle in his account. What is a sensible next step?
o: Keep it all as cash at home, where he can see it
Learn how a simple, low-cost option works and start small for the long term
Put everything into whatever his passengers say is rising fast
ask.why: Saved money can grow over time when it is put to work in options he understands. Learning first and starting small keeps the risk sensible, with an emergency amount kept aside. Cash at home earns nothing, and following passenger tips means betting on things he does not understand.

chapters.take: Saved money should not sit idle. Put it to work in ways you understand.

story.b: One night at the airport taxi stand, a fellow driver adds Sunil to a WhatsApp group. The messages are exciting. Screenshots of profits, voice notes from happy members, and a promise that any amount will double in thirty days. Ganesh has already put in twenty thousand rupees and says he received a small profit in the first week. Sunil feels the pull. His SIP seems so slow next to this. Then he remembers Divya's warning about anything that promises impossible returns. He calls her the next morning. She asks him a few simple questions about who runs the scheme and how it makes money. Sunil cannot answer any of them. He leaves the group that afternoon.

ask.q: A group promises to double Sunil's money in thirty days, and his friend says it works. What should Sunil do?
o: Ask someone experienced with nothing to sell him, and stay away if he cannot understand it
Put in a small amount first to test whether it is real
Put in a large amount quickly before the offer closes
ask.why: Promises of impossibly high returns are a warning sign, and early small profits are often used to pull people in deeper. A small test amount can still be lost, and rushing in is exactly what such schemes want. Advice from someone experienced who gains nothing protects him.

chapters.take: Protect what you have. If a return sounds impossible, it probably is.

story.b: Ganesh never gets his twenty thousand back, and Sunil quietly helps him with a small loan for his rent. The episode makes Sunil think about the other side of money, earning more. He notices that drivers who take tourists on weekend trips to Mysuru and Coorg earn far more per day. They speak basic English and know the history of each stop. So Sunil spends thirty minutes a day in the airport queue practising English with a free app and reading about the palaces and hill towns on the route. He also takes a simple health insurance plan for his family, after asking Divya to explain it. In two months, he books his first weekend tourist trip.

ask.q: Sunil wants to earn more without working longer hours. What is the best move?
o: Drive two extra hours every night, even when exhausted
Wait for the cab company to raise its rates
Learn skills like basic English and route knowledge that open better-paid trips
ask.why: Building skills raises what each hour of work is worth, and that keeps paying for years. Driving longer while exhausted is risky and has a hard limit, and waiting for the company to raise rates leaves his income in someone else's hands.

chapters.take: Your ability to earn is your biggest asset. Keep growing it.

story.b: A year later, Sunil still drives the same white sedan, but his money tells a different story. Every Monday, a tenth of his payout moves out before he spends a rupee. His daughter's school fees for next year are already sitting in a fixed deposit. His small SIP keeps running quietly, and he has stopped checking it every week. Two or three weekends a month, he drives tourists to Mysuru, telling them stories about the palace in careful English. Midnight biryani is now a Friday treat, and it tastes better for being rare. When a new double-your-money message arrives on his phone, he deletes it without opening it and goes back to reading about Coorg.

chapters.take: Wealth is built from small habits kept month after month, not from lucky breaks.
